title: MB7-09130
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of India who alleges that, should he be required to return to that country, he would face persecution, a risk to his life and a danger of torture and of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. He alleges that he fell in love with a young woman, XXXX, from the same village and the same XXXX XXXX family in XXXX or XXXX 2013, and that they were involved in a love affair they had to hide from their families. The appellant alleges that in XXXX 2013, his uncle saw the couple together at their friend's home and the uncle told the appellant's father, who became very angry and apparently threatened and beat the appellant to try to force him to end the relationship. The appellant's father and uncle supposedly went to see XXXX family to inform them, and this led the young woman's father to beat her. The appellant and the young woman pursued their relationship through a female friend. Following that, between XXXX 2013 and XXXX 2014, the appellant was apparently beaten several times by his family and the police. On XXXX XXXX, 2014, the appellant and XXXX supposedly decided to run away to Haryana so they could start a new life together. One of the young woman's uncles, being XXXX XXXX XXXX, was able to find them in Haryana and bring them back to the village. The appellant alleges that he was beaten by the police and accused of kidnapping XXXX, as well as drug trafficking. The XXXX was allegedly also angry with the appellant. In XXXX 2014, XXXX brother and a gang of his friends allegedly beat up the appellant with the intent to kill him, but at the last minute a passerby supposedly came to his aid. Next, in XXXX 2014, XXXX brother apparently fired at the appellant, but missed his target and hit the appellant's turban. The appellant fled the country to go to Australia, where he had obtained a study permit. He claims that in XXXX 2017, he ran into XXXX brother in a restaurant in Australia and therefore fled to Canada, where he was refused entry the first time in February 2017, but he was admitted on his second attempt in April 2017 and filed a claim for refugee protection upon arrival.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the appellant's refugee protection claim because it found that the appellant's allegations were not credible, and it also found that the appellant could benefit from an internal flight alternative (IFA) in New Delhi, Mumbai, and Calcutta. [1]

On appeal, the appellant contends that the RPD erred by breaching the principles of procedural fairness in two ways, that it should have conducted a separate analysis of the refugee protection claim from the perspective of section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), and that it failed to conduct a state protection analysis. The appellant also claims that the RPD erred when assessing his credibility and in its analysis of the proposed IFA.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) listened to the hearing recording and reviewed the RPD and appellant records to complete an independent analysis of all evidence in light of the appellant's arguments. After analyzing the Appeal Book, although the RAD does not agree that the RPD erred in terms of procedural fairness or the necessity of conducting a separate analysis of the appellant's fear under section 97, as well as a state protection analysis, the RAD agrees with the appellant's arguments that the RPD erred in its analysis of the credibility of the appellant's allegations, and in its analysis of the proposed IFA.
The appeal is allowed. The RAD refers the matter back for reconsideration by a differently constituted RPD panel.

The RAD must conduct a detailed, in-depth, comprehensive and independent review of the evidence introduced in light of the appellant's arguments on appeal.1 Although the appellant maintains that the RAD must apply the standard of reasonableness,2 the RAD must rather apply a standard of correctness to questions of fact, issues of mixed law and fact, and legal issues.3 ANALYSIS
paragraphs.heading_before: SCOPE OF THE APPEAL BEFORE THE RAD

paragraphs.text: The RAD will begin with an analysis of the appellant's arguments concerning (i) procedural fairness, (ii) the appellant's fear under section 97 of the IRPA, and (iii) the fact that the RPD did not address state protection. Next, the RAD will assess the credibility findings drawn by the RPD. Lastly, the RAD will address the IFA. i. Procedural fairness

With respect to procedural fairness, the appellant claims that the RPD (i) relied on its specialized knowledge to find that the torture and threats to which he had been subjected were not credible without providing him with notice and the opportunity to respond to that opinion;4 and (ii) by declaring that it would have, in any event, rejected the refugee protection claim in paragraph 22, the RPD displayed an appearance of bias.5

As for the RPD using its specialized knowledge, the RAD cannot accept this argument. First, the RAD notes that the appellant does not specify where in the decision the RPD declares having used its specialized knowledge, or where in the decision there is an allusion to its specialized knowledge. Second, after listening to the hearing recording, the RAD is unable to identify that the RPD relied on its specialized knowledge. Third, nowhere in the decision does the RAD find a sentence that makes a direct or indirect reference, or a reference that suggests that the RPD used its specialized knowledge to find that the appellant's allegations of torture were not credible. Consequently, the RAD finds that there was no breach of procedural fairness on this point.

Regarding the allegation that the RPD displayed an appearance of bias in paragraph 22 of its decision, the RAD cannot accept this argument either. The sentence cited by the appellant cannot be read out of context. The entire section preceding the sentence indicates that the RPD did not find the appellant's arguments credible.6 The RPD then states that even if it accepted the allegations as credible, it would have rejected the claim in any event, specifying that it is because it considers that the appellant has an IFA in Mumbai, Calcutta and New Delhi.7 Next, the decision proceeds with the reasons supporting its conclusion that there is an existing IFA for the appellant.8 The RAD therefore concludes that there was no appearance of bias by the RPD and that there was no breach of procedural fairness. ii. Fear under section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

The appellant maintains that the RPD should have considered his refugee protection claim from the perspective of section 97 of the IRPA, given that he had conveyed distinct reasons to fear returning to India, and it should have provided distinct reasons under section 97.9 The RAD does not agree with the appellant on this point. The RPD indeed based its decision to reject the appellant's refugee protection claim primarily on the lack of credibility of the appellant's allegations. Given the fact that it did not accept the appellant's allegations, the RPD was not required to conduct a separate analysis and provide distinct reasons for the rejection under section 97. Lack of credibility can be grounds for rejection under sections 96 and 97. The RAD therefore finds that the RPD did not err when it did not base its decision to reject the appellant's refugee protection claim under section 97 on distinct reasons. iii. State protection

Finally, the appellant contends that the RPD erred in failing to conduct an analysis of state protection, which is a determinative issue in his refugee protection claim given that his credibility was not seriously undermined.10 Again, the RAD does not accept the appellant's argument on this point. The RPD found, firstly, that the credibility of the appellant's allegations was the determinative issue. As it did not accept the appellant's allegations as credible, the RPD had no obligation to conduct a state protection analysis. Furthermore, the RPD alternatively found that, even if the appellant's allegations were credible, he could still benefit from an IFA in Calcutta, New Delhi and Mumbai. The IFA is also a determinative issue and therefore, if the RPD found that the appellant did not face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a risk to his life in the proposed IFA, there was no need for the RPD to consider state protection. The RAD therefore finds that the RPD did not err when it did not raise the issue of state protection in India in its decision. Credibility

The RPD identified the following issues with the credibility of the appellant's allegations in the decision: - After the Minister's intervention, which drew attention to a problem with dates, the appellant changed the dates of the events so they would be better aligned with his account. - He never alleged that he feared returning to India or going to Australia on his first visit to Canada. - On his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the appellant omitted the fact that he received threats by telephone from XXXX brother while he was living in Australia. - When he returned to Australia for XXXX months, the appellant did not file a refugee protection claim and did not move to another part of Australia to protect himself from XXXX brother. - The RPD found the appellant's explanations to justify the above-mentioned credibility issues to be inadequate. - The appellant provided no proof of the objective existence of XXXX or that XXXX uncle is a XXXX XXXX

The appellant submits that the RPD erred in its analysis of his credibility because: - it should not have rejected his testimony based on the differences between his statements on his visa application and his subsequent statements at the point of entry;11 - it was not clear enough in finding that the appellant's profile is not consistent with that of someone who truly fears for his life and, in any event, this is peripheral to the claim and cannot cause the claim to be rejected;12 and - it was unclear with respect to the allegations it found not to be credible and those it found to be credible, and the fact that it rendered a decision based on the IFA suggests that the reason for the rejection was not lack of credibility, but rather the IFA.13

First, the RAD notes that the RPD erred in finding that the appellant omitted on his BOC Form that XXXX brother was threatening him by telephone while he was in Australia. The RAD notes that it is indeed stated on the BOC Form.14

Second, the RPD notes in the decision that there was no objective evidence to establish that XXXX exists, but the RAD notes that the appellant provided three affidavits to corroborate his allegations and that the affidavits originated from third parties. More specifically, the affidavit by XXXX XXXX comes from a female friend who states that she has known XXXX for seven years, that she helped the couple to remain in contact in India and that she knows the complete history of their relationship together.15 The affidavit by XXXX XXXX(who specifies that he is a close friend of the appellant's father) and the appellant's neighbour's affidavit state that they know that the appellant had a romantic relationship with XXXX and that the relationship caused him problems with her family and the police.16 The RAD is therefore of the opinion that XXXX existence has been established and that the RPD erred on this point.

Third, the RPD did not question the applicant about the absence of evidence that XXXX uncle was XXXX XXXX XXXX, or that it was calling that information into question. This is also an error. If it had wished to fault the applicant for this lack of evidence, the RPD should have asked the appellant if he had any evidence of that or inquired as to the reason he had not filed evidence to that effect, particularly as the RPD is generally required to confront claimants with issues and consider explanations provided before drawing a conclusion on which it will base its decision.

However, the RAD does not agree with the appellant's argument that the RPD was not clear with respect to the allegations it considered to be credible and those it considered to not be credible. The RAD finds that the RPD clearly wrote in the decision that it considered the following allegations to not be credible: (1) The encounter with XXXX brother in Australia - The RPD observed that faced with the Minister's intervention, which called into question the date of this encounter and the time at which the date of the encounter was amended to show an earlier date on the BOC Form after the Minister's intervention, and the fact that his explanation was based on an interpretation that he declared false despite the fact that the appellant could read English; (2) The appellant's failure to state, upon his first attempt to enter Canada in February 2017, that he feared returning to India and to Australia, and his other statements that led the officers to believe that he simply sought entry to work, and the RPD preferred the officers' version over that of the appellant; (3) The fact that he returned to the same city in Australia where he had run into XXXX brother, and stayed there for XXXX months before returning a second time to Canada; (4) The RPD found that because it did not believe his allegations that he ran into the brother in XXXX 2016 or that the brother had threatened him in Australia, his other allegations of fear to return to India were undermined. (5) The RPD noted that he had no evidence of XXXX existence or that XXXX uncle was a XXXX XXXX; and (6) The fact that he did not file a claim for refugee protection in Australia in the XXXX years he lived there before fleeing to Canada.

Ultimately, the RAD notes that the RPD's credibility findings are primarily based on events that, according to the appellant, took place after he fled from India, as well as on his failure to file a refugee protection claim in Australia, all of which are peripheral factors. The RAD agrees with the RPD's reasoning with respect to the fact that the appellant amended the date of the encounter with XXXX brother in the restaurant in Australia after the Minister's intervention, that his explanation for the amendment did not adequately justify the change, and that the amendment affected the credibility of the allegation that he ran into the brother. Moreover, as for the parts of the decision that deal with the fact that the appellant made statements in Canada on his first visit to Canada in February 2017 that are not consistent with his allegations of fear in India and Australia, the RAD finds that he provided adequate explanations-he was advised by the officer who helped him obtain the visa for Canada to not file a refugee protection claim before entering Canada, and he felt intimidated by the officers at the airport because of their words and their behaviour toward him-to justify the fact that he acted as such on his first visit to Canada to claim refugee protection. Although the RAD agrees with the RPD that the appellant's failure to claim refugee protection in Australia for XXXX years before the encounter with XXXX brother in the restaurant and the fact that the appellant returned to the same city in Australia where he saw XXXX brother after he was denied entry to Canada are aspects of the appellant's case that did indeed have a negative impact on the credibility of the appellant's allegations, and the RAD finds that they had an impact on the appellant's subjective fear, they are not sufficient cause in themselves to reject the appellant's refugee protection claim.
Therefore, the RAD must analyze the RPD's conclusions with respect to the proposed IFA. Internal flight alternative

In his appeal, the appellant maintains that the RPD erred in its assessment of the IFA because it did not clearly indicate which allegations were credible and which were not.17 Furthermore, the appellant claims that he filed several pieces of evidence that the agents of persecution had the will and/or the capacity to find him, and that this evidence was ignored by the RPD.18

When the RPD considered the IFA issue, it stated "even if the claimant were to be found credible by the Tribunal," which demonstrates that for the purposes of the IFA analysis, it accepted that the appellant's allegations were credible. When the RPD considered the IFA, it mentioned the fact that the appellant alleges that XXXX uncle is a XXXX XXXX, but does not seem to have taken the allegation into consideration in its analysis. The RAD observes that neither did the RPD consider the appellant's claims that when he and XXXX fled the Punjab to hide together in Haryana, XXXX uncle, who is a XXXX XXXX, found out from XXXX XXXX XXXX where the couple was hiding, that the police arrested him in Haryana, and that the police accused him of kidnapping, beat him, and detained him for two days. If the RPD had taken these allegations into consideration, the RAD observes that the RPD should have addressed the allegations in the decision because they are inconsistent with its conclusion that the appellant could not be found in the proposed IFA, and that the RPD should have explained the reasons for which it nevertheless concluded that he could not be found or, otherwise, it could have allowed the appellant's refugee protection claim due to the absence of an IFA. Therefore, the RAD finds that the RPD erred when not taking into consideration all of the evidence before it during its IFA analysis.

In an effort to provide finality, the RAD sent a notice to the appellants on March 7, 2019, to invite them to provide their observations with respect to an IFA in Mumbai, Calcutta or New Delhi, and further to an update of the National Documentation Package (NDP) on India dated December 4, 2018, to give them the opportunity to provide additional observations with respect to the new NDP documents. The RAD received the appellant's response on March 14, 2019, and the response is now part of the appeal record before the RAD.

After having read the appellant's additional submissions, the RAD concludes that it cannot retain several parts of the submissions because they are not related to the allegations the appellant put forward on his BOC Form or in his testimony. More specifically, the appellant never claimed he had been arrested, detained and tortured by the police because he supported and collaborated with Sikh militants. The appellant never claimed that the XXXX intervened to help him get released from custody. He did not state that the police took his photo and his fingerprints, or that they made him sign a blank sheet of paper while in custody, and he did not state that he was ordered by the police to provide information on Sikh militants, or else he would have to report to the police station once a month.19 The RAD also notes that the submissions dealing with political opposition are also not applicable to this case, given that the appellant did not raise any fear of a political nature.20 The RAD concludes that the appellant's additional submissions did not fill in the gaps sufficiently so that the RAD could provide finality in the appellant's refugee protection claim.

Nevertheless, the RAD must mention that it noted an inconsistency between the appellant's allegations regarding the fact that XXXX uncle is XXXX XXXX XXXX, as he stated on his BOC Form that XXXX uncle was XXXX XXXX XXXX,21 but the close friend of XXXX affidavit states that XXXX family has ties with and influence over the police, without stating that a member of her family is XXXX XXXX XXXX.22 Given that the RPD did not ask any questions during the hearing about what happened in India to test the credibility of the allegations central to his refugee protection claim, or about the role of XXXX uncle with the XXXXor XXXX family's influence over the XXXX to test the viability of the proposed IFA, the RAD has no choice but to allow the appellant's appeal and refer the matter back to a differently constituted panel of the RPD for reconsideration of the appellant's refugee protection claim.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to a differently constituted panel of the RPD with the following directions: * The panel must be differently constituted; and * During the new hearing, the panel must ask questions about events that took place in India and XXXX family's ties to the XXXX, as well as any other question that would help the RPD render its decision.
